title: Coral and the Debt
premise: Oscar Vasquez, a crash investigator who survived the accident that killed his family in row twelve, has spent years hiding behind a polished lie and a packed go-bag. When the safe house protecting him is listed for sale online — complete with interior photos — he realizes someone inside the protection program is selling him out, and the buyer isn't looking for a witness: they're recruiting him for a staged aviation disaster timed to Frankfurt's market open. Forced to choose between the loyalty of the man who saved him and the truth about row twelve, Oscar goes off-grid to stop an attack designed to look like an accident, uncovering that his own survival was purchased as part of the plan. In the end, he exposes the conspiracy through a public crash hearing, trading his anonymity and his freedom for justice outside the law.
about_author: Theo Thornbury is a former insurance risk analyst who spent a decade reconstructing transportation disasters before turning to fiction full-time. He writes from a coastal town whose name he declines to share, drawing on case files he probably shouldn't have kept.

chapters.title: Row Twelve
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A sleepless night in the safe house; he rehearses his cover story while touching the go-bag by the door. Flashbacks to pulling his daughter's seatbelt buckle from the wreckage. Emotional beat: grief worn smooth into routine, and the first crack — a realtor's listing email arrives with photos of rooms only he should know.

chapters.title: The Listing
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He verifies the photos are current — taken within days, from inside. His handler, Marsh, dismisses it as a database error, but Oscar notices the camera angle matches the hallway where the program stores its master files. Emotional beat: paranoia sharpening into certainty that the leak is institutional, not accidental.

chapters.title: Marsh
chapters.summary: Dual POV: Oscar and Marsh. Marsh meets his own superior, Deputy Director Calloway, who orders Oscar relocated anyway — suspiciously fast. Marsh hesitates, remembering why he pulled Oscar from the program's worst failure years ago. Emotional beat: loyalty beginning to strain against duty on both sides.

chapters.title: Go-Bag
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He runs, following protocol he helped write, but every fallback contact is dead or reassigned. He realizes the relocation order would put him on a charter flight — Flight 4471 to Frankfurt via Reykjavik. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing he is the quarry, and the quarry is being herded.

chapters.title: The Man Who Bought the House
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He traces the listing to a shell LLC and confronts the broker, Lena Voss, who admits she was paid to photograph the interior by a 'security consultant' named Ilya Brandt. Emotional beat: the sick recognition that his sanctuary was staged like a set — someone wanted him comfortable before the cut.

chapters.title: What Survives a Crash
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, flashback-heavy. He reconstructs the original accident report and finds what he buried: the black-box data he certified was altered, and row twelve's seats were swapped two days before the flight. Emotional beat: guilt curdling — his polished lie protected whoever changed those seats.

chapters.title: Lena
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She decides Oscar is worth more alive than the fee Brandt offered for one more errand, and hands over a burner phone with a single text thread: coordinates, dates, and the phrase 'market open.' Emotional beat: a bystander choosing a side, terrified and resolute.

chapters.title: Calloway's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Calloway's POV. We learn the attack: a short position against a Frankfurt-listed insurer, triggered by a 'mechanical' crash of Flight 4471 carrying three executives. Oscar's death aboard it closes the loop on the old investigation. Emotional beat: cold bureaucratic evil — murder as line items.

chapters.title: Dead Drop
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He contacts Marsh through an old signal and gets burned — the meet is watched. Marsh arrives anyway, takes a beating covering Oscar's escape, and slips him a keycard to the program's evidence vault. Emotional beat: loyalty choosing truth at personal cost.

chapters.title: The Vault
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Inside the vault he finds the original black-box readout, a maintenance order signed with his own forged authorization code, and a personnel file proving his survival was flagged as 'asset retained' the day after the crash. Emotional beat: devastation — even his rescue was inventory.

chapters.title: Ilya Brandt
chapters.summary: Brandt's POV. The fixer prepares the aircraft: a sabotaged fuel sensor calibrated to fail at cruise altitude, deniable and slow enough for the pilots to be blamed. He notes Oscar's escape as a manageable variable. Emotional beat: professional calm masking contempt for everyone he's paid to betray.

chapters.title: Reykjavik
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He reaches Iceland ahead of the flight, posing as a maintenance contractor, and finds the tampered sensor — but photographing it trips a hangar alarm. Emotional beat: triumph flipping to exposure, running again with proof he can't yet use.

chapters.title: Grounded
chapters.summary: Marsh's POV. Hospitalized, Marsh leaks the flight manifest to a journalist, Dana Okafor, betting publicity is the only armor left. Calloway moves up the timeline. Emotional beat: a career man burning his own institution to save one person.

chapters.title: Dana
chapters.summary: Dana's POV. She verifies the manifest anomaly and the shell LLC, then faces her editor's lawyers and kills the story — for now — but copies everything to a dead-man switch. Emotional beat: the lonely arithmetic of truth in a newsroom afraid of libel.

chapters.title: Boarding
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. He boards Flight 4471 under a contractor badge, planning to force a ground stop, and comes face to face with Brandt in the jet bridge. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into purpose — he boards the plane meant to be his coffin.

chapters.title: Four Hours to Frankfurt
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, claustrophobic and ticking. He can't reach the avionics bay without credentials; instead he triggers a maintenance fault warning and quietly evacuates rows near the executives, buying time. Emotional beat: a man saving strangers in the seats where his family died.

chapters.title: Diversion
chapters.summary: Cockpit and Oscar POV intercut. The captain diverts to Hamburg after Oscar's planted fault cascades; Brandt realizes the sabotage will be found intact and moves to destroy evidence mid-flight. Emotional beat: the attack failing not with explosions but with paperwork and nerve.

chapters.title: Row Twelve, Again
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Brandt corners him in the aft galley; in the struggle, Oscar pins him against the very seat model from the old crash and forces him to confess on Dana's live-open recorder hidden in the cabin. Emotional beat: rage mastered into testimony — the confession captured, not the kill taken.

chapters.title: Hamburg
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The plane lands; police swarm; Brandt is arrested but Calloway's name surfaces nowhere. Marsh, discharged early, delivers the vault keycard to investigators anonymously. Emotional beat: victory that feels incomplete — the hand stayed hidden.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. At the emergency safety hearing, Oscar discards his cover identity publicly, presenting the original black-box data and the 'asset retained' file. Dana's dead-man switch publishes simultaneously. Emotional beat: the lie finally set down like a heavy bag.

chapters.title: Calloway
chapters.summary: Calloway's POV collapsing into Oscar's. Exposed by the published files and Marsh's sworn statement, Calloway is indicted; he offers Oscar a deal — silence for reinstatement — and Oscar refuses. Emotional beat: justice chosen over comfort, at last, without flinching.

chapters.title: Unpacked
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, epilogue. Months later, Oscar testifies under his real name, visits the graves in row twelve's memorial garden, and unpacks the go-bag for the first time — keeping only his daughter's recovered buckle. Lena sends a postcard; Marsh retires. Emotional beat: survival redefined — not escaping the past, but finally paying its debt and staying.
